[2] The Appellants' claims were heard by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on December 18, 2019 and rejected on January 27, 2020. The determinative issue was the existence of viable internal flight alternatives (IFAs) in Port Harcourt, Benin City, and Ibadan.

[3] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in finding Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851 applicable in their circumstances and erred in its analyses of both prongs of the test for an IFA.1 After perfection of the appeal, I notified the Appellants by Member's Direction2 that I would be considering the evidence in the current National Documentation Package (NDP) for Nigeria.3 The Appellants argue that the Revocation of Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851,4 as of April 6, 2020, removes the basis for the RPD's decision and, therefore, their claims should be accepted by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellants also argue that the updated evidence of country conditions supports their position that they do not have a viable IFA.5
DECISION

[4] The appeal is allowed. I find that the Appellants do not have a viable IFA and they have established their claims. I substitute my own decision that the Appellants are Convention refugees.
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

They allege that they cannot return to Nigeria because they fear the family of the Principal Appellant's deceased partner, who was also the father of the Minor Appellants. The Appellants allege that his family will kill or harm the Principal Appellant, remove the Minor Appellants from her custody, subject the female Minor Appellant to female genital mutilation (FGM), and forcibly convert the male Minor Appellant to Islam.

[2] The Appellants' claims were heard by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on December 18, 2019 and rejected on January 27, 2020. The determinative issue was the existence of viable internal flight alternatives (IFAs) in Port Harcourt, Benin City, and Ibadan.

[3] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in finding Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851 applicable in their circumstances and erred in its analyses of both prongs of the test for an IFA.1 After perfection of the appeal, I notified the Appellants by Member's Direction2 that I would be considering the evidence in the current National Documentation Package (NDP) for Nigeria.3 The Appellants argue that the Revocation of Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851,4 as of April 6, 2020, removes the basis for the RPD's decision and, therefore, their claims should be accepted by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellants also argue that the updated evidence of country conditions supports their position that they do not have a viable IFA.5
DECISION

[4] The appeal is allowed. I find that the Appellants do not have a viable IFA and they have established their claims. I substitute my own decision that the Appellants are Convention refugees.
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

[5] The role of the RAD is to look at all the evidence and decide whether the RPD made the correct decision.6 I find that the RPD had no meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral evidence. Therefore, the standard of review is correctness.

[6] Because the claims include allegations of gender-related fear of persecution, I have assessed the evidence while keeping in mind Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.7

subthemes.text:
[7] The determinative issues in this appeal are as follows:
a. The Appellants do not have a viable IFA.
b. The presumption of truthfulness has not been rebutted, therefore, the Appellants have established their allegations, on a balance of probabilities.
c. The Appellants meet the definition of Convention refugee, as set out in section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).8
The legal test for IFA

[8] There are two prongs to the legal test for a viable IFA. First, it must be determined that, in the IFA location, there is no serious possibility of persecution and, on a balance of probabilities, no risk under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, meaning no danger of torture, risk to life, or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Secondly, it must not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those personal to the claimant, to relocate there. The standard is high and requires proof of adverse conditions that would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant in travelling to and living in the IFA location. Both prongs must be satisfied for a finding that there is an IFA.9

[9] On an independent assessment, I find that updated evidence of country conditions establishes that, on a balance of probabilities, it would be unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to any of the proposed IFA locations. Therefore, I do not find it necessary to consider the Appellants' arguments in relation to the first prong of the test for an IFA.
On a balance of probabilities, an IFA for the Appellants is not objectively reasonable

[10] In assessing the viability of the IFA locations, the RPD applied the reasoning in Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851. The Appellants argue that the subsequent Revocation of Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851 means that the RPD's decision cannot stand.10 I do not agree that the Revocation of the Guide is, on its own, a reason to overturn the RPD's decision. However, I agree with the Appellants that findings based on country conditions that have changed must be reconsidered. While no longer a Jurisprudential Guide, RAD Decision TB7-19851 still provides a useful conceptual framework of analysis for considering the viability of an IFA for persons fleeing non-state actors in Nigeria. In conducting my independent assessment, I have considered the evidence in the record and in the most recent NDP. I have accepted the Principal Appellant's evidence that she is a single mother, with two young children; her parents and only sibling are deceased; and she has no family support in Nigeria. I accept the Appellants' argument that the RPD's decision cannot stand because I have concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants do not have an objectively reasonable IFA. In the reasons that follow, I explain why I have concluded that the evidence weighs against the viability of an IFA.
Education and employment

[11] The RPD found that the evidence was insufficient to suggest that the challenges the Principal Appellant would face in seeking employment would outweigh the positive factors in her educational and employment background.11 The Appellants argue that the evidence in the current NDP establishes that this conclusion is incorrect. I agree with the Appellants.

[12] The Principal Appellant's evidence is that she has 12 years of education, including six years in high school.12 This is above the average educational standard of Nigerian women.13 However, her employment experience is limited. The Principal Appellant's evidence is that, as a 14-year-old, after her parents died and she became homeless, she began "hawking" vegetables on the streets of Lagos for a woman who provided her with shelter in exchange.14 She stopped doing this when she moved in with her now-deceased partner and then, for about five and a half years, until he died, she sold skincare products from the home that they shared.15 The Principal Appellant testified that "hawking" is not legal and requires evading enforcement authorities.16 She also testified that, without any funding, she would not be able to start another business selling beauty supplies and finding a job, as a single mother with limited education and work experience, would be a big challenge.17

[13] The RPD found that there was insufficient evidence to establish that the Principal Appellant would not be able to secure any employment in the IFA locations or obtain any funding to restart her beauty business.18 The Appellants argue that the RPD erred. I agree. On an independent assessment of the evidence, my conclusions differ from those of the RPD. The RPD's reasons state that the Principal Appellant's evidence is that she survived independently without assistance from family since XXXX 2000 and that she received support from a friend and from her late partner's friend after she died.19 The Principal Appellant's evidence was that, in XXXX 2010 until his death on XXXX XXXX, 2017, she lived with her late partner and they had two children together during this time. The evidence is that he was from a wealthy family, he was employed, and he rented the home they lived in.20 I do not find that the evidence supports the inference that the Principal Appellant survived independently during this time; rather, it indicates that her late partner supported her and their children. Although the Appellants stayed with the Principal Appellant's friend before they left Lagos, I find it speculative to suggest that the same friend would be able and willing to lend money to the Principal Appellant to start a business in an IFA location. There is evidence that the late partner's friend who assisted the Appellants to leave Nigeria has financial resources. However, I do not find that his willingness to help them leave Nigeria in the wake of the late partner's death is a sufficient basis for inferring that he would be willing to provide financial support for the Principal Appellant to start a business in a new location, on her own, while raising her children.

[14] The independent documentary evidence is that women are often disadvantaged in access to employment opportunities and in conditions of work and that they participate more in the informal economy.21 There is a high rate of unemployment in Nigeria and many Nigerians live in extreme poverty, with women's disadvantageous position in the labour market being a significant factor in their overrepresentation among the poor.22 Employment prospects for people relocating to cities in Nigeria are best for those with skills and experience.23 As well, female headed households often rely on social networks from family or communities for their survival.24

[15] There is evidence that, without support, surviving anywhere in Nigeria is very difficult for women heads of households.25 I do not find that the Principal Appellant's profile and background put her in a favourable position to support herself and her children financially.

[16] Adding to my concern is the documentary evidence which indicates that female heads of households seeking employment may be the targets of sexual exploitation.26 The Principal Appellant has alleged that, as a child, she was the victim of sexual abuse.27 That allegation is not relevant to the forward-facing risk on which the Appellants' claims are based, but it forms part of the Principal Appellant's personal circumstances and is a risk factor that increases her vulnerability to sexual coercion.28
Access to housing

[17] Women have more difficulty accessing housing in Nigeria if they do not have a male partner or a man who is willing to pose as one.29 There is a lack of adequate housing and access is dependent on income.30 I find that, given the poor prospects for the Principal Appellant's employment and the absence of family support, the Appellants will likely face significant barriers accessing adequate accommodation.
Access to health care

[18] The Principal Appellant testified that, after her late partner died, she refrained from seeking medical treatment for herself because she preferred to use what money she had to feed her children.31 Access to adequate health care in Nigeria depends largely on financial resources.32 Absent employment that would enable the Principal Appellant to support herself and her children, the evidence is that, on a balance of probabilities, they would not be able to get health care.
On a balance of probabilities, relocation in Nigeria is objectively unreasonable for the Appellants

[19] The threshold for the objectively unreasonable standard is very high and requires, at a minimum, actual and concrete evidence of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the Appellants in relocating to a safe area.33 I find that, in the Appellants' circumstances, the evidence meets this threshold, on a balance of probabilities. The evidence establishes that the Principal Appellant is a single mother with limited work experience and no family support in Nigeria. The independent documentary evidence is sufficient for me to conclude that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants would face undue hardship in any of the IFA locations, given the barriers they would face in accessing the necessities of life, including food and shelter.
The Appellants meet the test for Convention refugees

subthemes.text:
[20] Having found that the Appellants do not have a viable internal flight alternative, I have reviewed the record and considered whether they qualify as Convention refugees. The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's responses to credibility concerns raised at the hearing were reasonable and plausible. The RPD accepted that she was generally credible except in relation to specific issues pertaining to the viability of an IFA.34 I have reviewed her testimony and other evidence on the record and I find no material issues with the credibility of the Appellants' allegations in support of their claims. The RPD did not identify any material inconsistencies or contradictions, nor do I. On an independent assessment, having regard to the presumption of truthfulness,35 I accept the Appellants' allegations, on a balance of probabilities.

[21] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on political opinion because she alleges that she fears persecution if she refuses to allow the female Minor Appellant to be subjected to FGM.36 I agree with the RPD that the Principal Appellant's opposition to FGM for her daughter constitutes a political opinion, in that it is an opinion about gender roles and behaviour which conflicts with social and cultural norms adhered to by the agent of persecution.37 I find this based on the Principal Appellant's evidence that she has been threatened with death by her late partner's father if she refuses to present her daughter for circumcision. The RPD found that the female Minor Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on her membership in the particular social group of girls fearing gender-related persecution.38 I agree. She is a girl who faces a serious risk of undergoing FGM, which constitutes persecution. The RPD found that the male Minor Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on religion because the risk he faces is forced conversion to Islam.39 I agree. The father of the Principal Appellant's late partner has threatened to take the Minor Appellants and place the male Minor Appellant in Arabic school and convert him to Islam. Forcible religious conversion constitutes persecution. The documentary evidence corroborates the objective foundation of the Appellants' fears. There is evidence that FGM occurs in Nigeria.40 There is evidence that customary laws may give the male head of a father's family the right to custody of his children upon his death.41

[19] The threshold for the objectively unreasonable standard is very high and requires, at a minimum, actual and concrete evidence of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the Appellants in relocating to a safe area.33 I find that, in the Appellants' circumstances, the evidence meets this threshold, on a balance of probabilities. The evidence establishes that the Principal Appellant is a single mother with limited work experience and no family support in Nigeria. The independent documentary evidence is sufficient for me to conclude that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants would face undue hardship in any of the IFA locations, given the barriers they would face in accessing the necessities of life, including food and shelter.
The Appellants meet the test for Convention refugees

[20] Having found that the Appellants do not have a viable internal flight alternative, I have reviewed the record and considered whether they qualify as Convention refugees. The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's responses to credibility concerns raised at the hearing were reasonable and plausible. The RPD accepted that she was generally credible except in relation to specific issues pertaining to the viability of an IFA.34 I have reviewed her testimony and other evidence on the record and I find no material issues with the credibility of the Appellants' allegations in support of their claims. The RPD did not identify any material inconsistencies or contradictions, nor do I. On an independent assessment, having regard to the presumption of truthfulness,35 I accept the Appellants' allegations, on a balance of probabilities.

[21] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on political opinion because she alleges that she fears persecution if she refuses to allow the female Minor Appellant to be subjected to FGM.36 I agree with the RPD that the Principal Appellant's opposition to FGM for her daughter constitutes a political opinion, in that it is an opinion about gender roles and behaviour which conflicts with social and cultural norms adhered to by the agent of persecution.37 I find this based on the Principal Appellant's evidence that she has been threatened with death by her late partner's father if she refuses to present her daughter for circumcision. The RPD found that the female Minor Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on her membership in the particular social group of girls fearing gender-related persecution.38 I agree. She is a girl who faces a serious risk of undergoing FGM, which constitutes persecution. The RPD found that the male Minor Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on religion because the risk he faces is forced conversion to Islam.39 I agree. The father of the Principal Appellant's late partner has threatened to take the Minor Appellants and place the male Minor Appellant in Arabic school and convert him to Islam. Forcible religious conversion constitutes persecution. The documentary evidence corroborates the objective foundation of the Appellants' fears. There is evidence that FGM occurs in Nigeria.40 There is evidence that customary laws may give the male head of a father's family the right to custody of his children upon his death.41

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and her children, XXXX XXXX XXXX (male Minor Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (female Minor Appellant) are citizens of Nigeria. They allege that they cannot return to Nigeria because they fear the family of the Principal Appellant's deceased partner, who was also the father of the Minor Appellants. The Appellants allege that his family will kill or harm the Principal Appellant, remove the Minor Appellants from her custody, subject the female Minor Appellant to female genital mutilation (FGM), and forcibly convert the male Minor Appellant to Islam.

[2] The Appellants' claims were heard by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on December 18, 2019 and rejected on January 27, 2020. The determinative issue was the existence of viable internal flight alternatives (IFAs) in Port Harcourt, Benin City, and Ibadan.

[3] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in finding Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851 applicable in their circumstances and erred in its analyses of both prongs of the test for an IFA.1 After perfection of the appeal, I notified the Appellants by Member's Direction2 that I would be considering the evidence in the current National Documentation Package (NDP) for Nigeria.3 The Appellants argue that the Revocation of Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851,4 as of April 6, 2020, removes the basis for the RPD's decision and, therefore, their claims should be accepted by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellants also argue that the updated evidence of country conditions supports their position that they do not have a viable IFA.5
DECISION

[4] The appeal is allowed. I find that the Appellants do not have a viable IFA and they have established their claims. I substitute my own decision that the Appellants are Convention refugees.
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

[5] The role of the RAD is to look at all the evidence and decide whether the RPD made the correct decision.6 I find that the RPD had no meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral evidence. Therefore, the standard of review is correctness.

[6] Because the claims include allegations of gender-related fear of persecution, I have assessed the evidence while keeping in mind Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.7
ANALYSIS

[7] The determinative issues in this appeal are as follows:
a. The Appellants do not have a viable IFA.
b. The presumption of truthfulness has not been rebutted, therefore, the Appellants have established their allegations, on a balance of probabilities.
c. The Appellants meet the definition of Convention refugee, as set out in section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).8
The legal test for IFA

[8] There are two prongs to the legal test for a viable IFA. First, it must be determined that, in the IFA location, there is no serious possibility of persecution and, on a balance of probabilities, no risk under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, meaning no danger of torture, risk to life, or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Secondly, it must not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those personal to the claimant, to relocate there. The standard is high and requires proof of adverse conditions that would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant in travelling to and living in the IFA location. Both prongs must be satisfied for a finding that there is an IFA.9

[9] On an independent assessment, I find that updated evidence of country conditions establishes that, on a balance of probabilities, it would be unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to any of the proposed IFA locations. Therefore, I do not find it necessary to consider the Appellants' arguments in relation to the first prong of the test for an IFA.
On a balance of probabilities, an IFA for the Appellants is not objectively reasonable

[10] In assessing the viability of the IFA locations, the RPD applied the reasoning in Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851. The Appellants argue that the subsequent Revocation of Jurisprudential Guide TB7-19851 means that the RPD's decision cannot stand.10 I do not agree that the Revocation of the Guide is, on its own, a reason to overturn the RPD's decision. However, I agree with the Appellants that findings based on country conditions that have changed must be reconsidered. While no longer a Jurisprudential Guide, RAD Decision TB7-19851 still provides a useful conceptual framework of analysis for considering the viability of an IFA for persons fleeing non-state actors in Nigeria. In conducting my independent assessment, I have considered the evidence in the record and in the most recent NDP. I have accepted the Principal Appellant's evidence that she is a single mother, with two young children; her parents and only sibling are deceased; and she has no family support in Nigeria. I accept the Appellants' argument that the RPD's decision cannot stand because I have concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants do not have an objectively reasonable IFA. In the reasons that follow, I explain why I have concluded that the evidence weighs against the viability of an IFA.
Education and employment

[11] The RPD found that the evidence was insufficient to suggest that the challenges the Principal Appellant would face in seeking employment would outweigh the positive factors in her educational and employment background.11 The Appellants argue that the evidence in the current NDP establishes that this conclusion is incorrect. I agree with the Appellants.

[12] The Principal Appellant's evidence is that she has 12 years of education, including six years in high school.12 This is above the average educational standard of Nigerian women.13 However, her employment experience is limited. The Principal Appellant's evidence is that, as a 14-year-old, after her parents died and she became homeless, she began "hawking" vegetables on the streets of Lagos for a woman who provided her with shelter in exchange.14 She stopped doing this when she moved in with her now-deceased partner and then, for about five and a half years, until he died, she sold skincare products from the home that they shared.15 The Principal Appellant testified that "hawking" is not legal and requires evading enforcement authorities.16 She also testified that, without any funding, she would not be able to start another business selling beauty supplies and finding a job, as a single mother with limited education and work experience, would be a big challenge.17

[13] The RPD found that there was insufficient evidence to establish that the Principal Appellant would not be able to secure any employment in the IFA locations or obtain any funding to restart her beauty business.18 The Appellants argue that the RPD erred. I agree. On an independent assessment of the evidence, my conclusions differ from those of the RPD. The RPD's reasons state that the Principal Appellant's evidence is that she survived independently without assistance from family since XXXX 2000 and that she received support from a friend and from her late partner's friend after she died.19 The Principal Appellant's evidence was that, in XXXX 2010 until his death on XXXX XXXX, 2017, she lived with her late partner and they had two children together during this time. The evidence is that he was from a wealthy family, he was employed, and he rented the home they lived in.20 I do not find that the evidence supports the inference that the Principal Appellant survived independently during this time; rather, it indicates that her late partner supported her and their children. Although the Appellants stayed with the Principal Appellant's friend before they left Lagos, I find it speculative to suggest that the same friend would be able and willing to lend money to the Principal Appellant to start a business in an IFA location. There is evidence that the late partner's friend who assisted the Appellants to leave Nigeria has financial resources. However, I do not find that his willingness to help them leave Nigeria in the wake of the late partner's death is a sufficient basis for inferring that he would be willing to provide financial support for the Principal Appellant to start a business in a new location, on her own, while raising her children.

[14] The independent documentary evidence is that women are often disadvantaged in access to employment opportunities and in conditions of work and that they participate more in the informal economy.21 There is a high rate of unemployment in Nigeria and many Nigerians live in extreme poverty, with women's disadvantageous position in the labour market being a significant factor in their overrepresentation among the poor.22 Employment prospects for people relocating to cities in Nigeria are best for those with skills and experience.23 As well, female headed households often rely on social networks from family or communities for their survival.24

[15] There is evidence that, without support, surviving anywhere in Nigeria is very difficult for women heads of households.25 I do not find that the Principal Appellant's profile and background put her in a favourable position to support herself and her children financially.

[16] Adding to my concern is the documentary evidence which indicates that female heads of households seeking employment may be the targets of sexual exploitation.26 The Principal Appellant has alleged that, as a child, she was the victim of sexual abuse.27 That allegation is not relevant to the forward-facing risk on which the Appellants' claims are based, but it forms part of the Principal Appellant's personal circumstances and is a risk factor that increases her vulnerability to sexual coercion.28
Access to housing

[17] Women have more difficulty accessing housing in Nigeria if they do not have a male partner or a man who is willing to pose as one.29 There is a lack of adequate housing and access is dependent on income.30 I find that, given the poor prospects for the Principal Appellant's employment and the absence of family support, the Appellants will likely face significant barriers accessing adequate accommodation.
Access to health care

[18] The Principal Appellant testified that, after her late partner died, she refrained from seeking medical treatment for herself because she preferred to use what money she had to feed her children.31 Access to adequate health care in Nigeria depends largely on financial resources.32 Absent employment that would enable the Principal Appellant to support herself and her children, the evidence is that, on a balance of probabilities, they would not be able to get health care.
On a balance of probabilities, relocation in Nigeria is objectively unreasonable for the Appellants

[19] The threshold for the objectively unreasonable standard is very high and requires, at a minimum, actual and concrete evidence of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the Appellants in relocating to a safe area.33 I find that, in the Appellants' circumstances, the evidence meets this threshold, on a balance of probabilities. The evidence establishes that the Principal Appellant is a single mother with limited work experience and no family support in Nigeria. The independent documentary evidence is sufficient for me to conclude that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants would face undue hardship in any of the IFA locations, given the barriers they would face in accessing the necessities of life, including food and shelter.
The Appellants meet the test for Convention refugees

[20] Having found that the Appellants do not have a viable internal flight alternative, I have reviewed the record and considered whether they qualify as Convention refugees. The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's responses to credibility concerns raised at the hearing were reasonable and plausible. The RPD accepted that she was generally credible except in relation to specific issues pertaining to the viability of an IFA.34 I have reviewed her testimony and other evidence on the record and I find no material issues with the credibility of the Appellants' allegations in support of their claims. The RPD did not identify any material inconsistencies or contradictions, nor do I. On an independent assessment, having regard to the presumption of truthfulness,35 I accept the Appellants' allegations, on a balance of probabilities.

[21] The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on political opinion because she alleges that she fears persecution if she refuses to allow the female Minor Appellant to be subjected to FGM.36 I agree with the RPD that the Principal Appellant's opposition to FGM for her daughter constitutes a political opinion, in that it is an opinion about gender roles and behaviour which conflicts with social and cultural norms adhered to by the agent of persecution.37 I find this based on the Principal Appellant's evidence that she has been threatened with death by her late partner's father if she refuses to present her daughter for circumcision. The RPD found that the female Minor Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on her membership in the particular social group of girls fearing gender-related persecution.38 I agree. She is a girl who faces a serious risk of undergoing FGM, which constitutes persecution. The RPD found that the male Minor Appellant's claim had a nexus to the Refugee Convention based on religion because the risk he faces is forced conversion to Islam.39 I agree. The father of the Principal Appellant's late partner has threatened to take the Minor Appellants and place the male Minor Appellant in Arabic school and convert him to Islam. Forcible religious conversion constitutes persecution. The documentary evidence corroborates the objective foundation of the Appellants' fears. There is evidence that FGM occurs in Nigeria.40 There is evidence that customary laws may give the male head of a father's family the right to custody of his children upon his death.41

[22] I have considered whether the Appellants have access to adequate state protection. On a balance of probabilities, I find that they do not. The Principal Appellant's evidence was that she approached the police and was told that since these were family issues they would not intervene and she should resolve it with the family.42 I accept this allegation, on a balance of probabilities. There is documentary evidence to support the allegation that police do not get involved in what they consider to be family matters.43 I have already explained my reasons for concluding that the Appellants do not have a viable IFA.

[23] Consequently, I find that the Appellants are Convention refugees as they have established that they face a serious possibility of persecution in Nigeria for reasons set out in section 96 of the IRPA and do not have access to adequate state protection or a viable IFA.
CONCLUSION

[24] The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, I set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute my own determination that the Appellants are Convention refugees.
